video_title: Scaling Laws: Child Safety AI Policy at Scale with Vaishnavi J and Dave Willner
gist: Zentropy's Dave Willner and Vice's Vaishnavi J explain open-source, age-banded teen AI safety policies enforced by small policy-following classifiers that were optimized automatically from about 1,200 labeled examples. They argue for age-appropriate design over bans, efficacy measurement of mandated interventions, and structural insulation of safety teams.

insights.claim: Zentropy builds classifiers that take a written policy text as input, so changing the policy text changes classifier behavior without the old pipeline of tens of thousands of human-labeled examples and a long retraining loop.
insights.speaker: Dave Willner
insights.so_what: Collapses the cost and latency of trust-and-safety policy iteration, opening a commercial niche for policy-following models.

insights.claim: Zentropy's special-purpose small language models match a GPT-5-class model on policy-following classification while being about two orders of magnitude smaller, with basic versions open source and runnable on a decent MacBook Pro.
insights.speaker: Dave Willner
insights.so_what: Small specialized models undercut frontier-model inference cost for high-volume moderation, a cost/latency moat argument for narrow models.

insights.claim: Because the small classifier is so fast, Zentropy built 'optimizers' that automatically rewrite a content policy and score each rewrite by how well the classifier reproduces human labels, turning policy writing into an empirical, testable process.
insights.speaker: Dave Willner
insights.so_what: Second-order product: speed of the base model enables meta-tooling (automated policy optimization) that slower, costlier models could not support.

insights.claim: Dave Willner had Claude browse X and gather examples of users asking Grok to undress photos, plus benign Grok requests, and with roughly 1,000 labeled examples and a couple of optimizer passes produced a published policy that was about 98% accurate at detecting nudification attempts, in a few hours over a weekend.
insights.speaker: Dave Willner
insights.so_what: Shows how cheap it is now to stand up a targeted classifier; the 98% figure is on easy, non-obfuscated data, so it is an upper-bound signal.

insights.claim: Willner argues xAI's Grok nonconsensual-intimate-image scandal was a choice, not a hard technical problem, since detecting nudification requests is an easy classification task and the platform was 'clearly not trying'.
insights.speaker: Dave Willner
insights.so_what: Frames regulatory and reputational risk for xAI as self-inflicted and cheaply avoidable, raising the bar for 'we couldn't prevent it' defenses.

insights.claim: For the optimizer approach, coverage matters more than volume: a representative set of around 1,000-1,200 labeled examples spanning the expected problem types works better than piling up more examples of the same kind.
insights.speaker: Dave Willner
insights.so_what: Lowers the data-labeling barrier to entry for new safety classifiers, reducing demand for large human-labeling operations.

insights.claim: Vice and Zentropy released open-source teen AI policies split into two age bands, 13-15 and 13-17 (skewed to older teens), with six policies in total and four enforcement types per band, each independently written and reassessed per age band.
insights.speaker: Vaishnavi J
insights.so_what: A concrete, forkable template that platforms facing teen-safety regulation can adopt as a baseline.

insights.claim: Age-banded scaffolding lowers the cost of inaccurate age-assurance: if a model misjudges a 16-year-old as 14, the teen simply gets the 13-15 experience rather than an all-or-nothing outcome, so age gating works more like a room with progressively more access than a switch.
insights.speaker: Vaishnavi J
insights.so_what: Argues that graded policies make imperfect age-estimation models regulatorily and practically viable.

insights.claim: Policies on suicide and self-injury must be reweighted by age because of competing effects: the Werther contagion effect should weigh more for younger teens, while the Papageno protective effect of help-seeking is more valuable for older teens, so each policy has to be reassessed per age band rather than simply made more or less conservative.
insights.speaker: Vaishnavi J
insights.so_what: Shows that uniform conservative rules can be counterproductive; granular age-specific tuning is the product requirement.

insights.claim: A June study cited by Vaishnavi (RAND and JAMA Pediatrics) found 63% of teens using chatbots for mental-health advice told no one, so full bans are unenforceable when use is invisible.
insights.speaker: Vaishnavi J
insights.so_what: Undercuts the ban-based regulatory model and favors design-level safeguards inside the products themselves.

insights.claim: The host cited Pew data (Feb 2026) that 36% of teens do not use AI chatbots, 57% of chatbot use is for searching information, 54% for schoolwork help and 12% for emotional support, and only 31% of 13-17 year olds expect AI's societal impact over 20 years to be positive versus 26% negative.
insights.speaker: Host (Scaling Laws)
insights.so_what: Teen emotional-support use is a minority but material share, and teen sentiment is skeptical, which shapes the regulatory climate.

insights.claim: Early evidence from the UK suggests teen social/AI bans are being circumvented, and age verification carries the tradeoff of sharing sensitive data with third parties who can be hacked.
insights.speaker: Host (Scaling Laws)
insights.so_what: Supports a policy shift toward age-appropriate design over bans and hard ID-based verification.

insights.claim: Laws increasingly mandate evaluations, protocols and interventions like parental controls or screen-time limits, but almost nobody measures whether those interventions work; Vaishnavi wants regulators to require efficacy measurement of the interventions themselves.
insights.speaker: Vaishnavi J
insights.so_what: Expect growing demand for independent evaluation and measurement vendors as compliance moves from 'did you ship it' to 'did it work'.

insights.claim: Snap publicly disclosed in 2024 that only 2% of US teens had parental controls turned on, and Vaishnavi says no other company would publish comparable figures.
insights.speaker: Vaishnavi J
insights.so_what: Low parental-control adoption weakens the regulatory case for control-based solutions and favors default-on safeguards.
insights.quote: only 2% of all US teens had parental controls turned on

insights.claim: Willner argues that after 15-20 years and many billions of dollars spent on trust and safety, the darker conclusion is that companies have tried fairly hard and the industry is simply not good at it, with useful research locked inside companies and discovery-risk incentives discouraging studies.
insights.speaker: Dave Willner
insights.so_what: Implies better tooling and public research, not just more spending or pressure, is the bottleneck.

insights.claim: Willner proposes that regulators focus on power dynamics inside companies, modeled on banks and airlines where safety teams are structurally insulated from commercial pressure, rather than prescriptive safety-practice rules or reporting forms that go stale in an adversarial space.
insights.speaker: Dave Willner
insights.so_what: A different regulatory design: governance and org-structure mandates could hit large platforms harder than disclosure-style rules; he expects big platforms to dislike it.

insights.claim: Vice and Zentropy open-sourced the policies and labeled dataset so platforms can fork them, revalidate against their own data and edit; Vaishnavi says clients will still need forked, customized versions, so giving the baseline away works as an easy entry point rather than charity.
insights.speaker: Vaishnavi J
insights.so_what: Open baseline as a customer-acquisition funnel for custom policy and classifier work.

insights.claim: ROOST (robust open source safety tools) is a community effort to provide baseline open classification systems and moderator review interfaces; both guests urge frontier labs to donate more open-source safety policies and classifiers, noting current public releases are binary and cover only about five or six categories.
insights.speaker: Vaishnavi J
insights.so_what: Shared safety infrastructure could commoditize basic trust-and-safety tooling, pushing vendor differentiation to product-specific tuning.

insights.claim: Willner describes policy work as gardening rather than reaching a perfect policy: the space is adversarial and socially shifting, so the goal is machinery that adapts faster with fewer human externalities.
insights.speaker: Dave Willner
insights.so_what: Favors vendors selling continuous adaptation over static rule sets or one-time compliance deliverables.
